blocks.x: This is an interview today at 832 North Galvest Street. Can I get your name?
Yeah, Joseph Watkins. And you? Barry Mountain.
And I'm Thick Allen. What's today's date?
The day is the 19th. Oh, 20th, Joe. Huh? 20th, ain't it today? No, yesterday was the 18th. I went up to the hospital yesterday. Was it the 19th? Was it the 18th? It's the 19th.
It's inauguration today. It's the 20th.
The 20th, that's right.
It's gotta be the 20th.
Yeah, inauguration. And you know where I had to buy that record? Where is that? In Boston.
Well, we didn't put the year. January 20th, 1961. That's right. Alright, go to it. I just want to get that on that first.
Yeah, let's put these down. Well, maybe you better begin by telling this your birth date.

October 24th. I was born in 1900, Chattery Hospital. And lived in the Third Ward quite a few years. Oh. Well, I've taken music inspiration from the different jazz brass bands they had around that ward. Not that particular ward. But several wards all had social and pleasure clubs. You had the Magnorias, you had the Pickles, you had the Taminets, and several other aid and pleasure clubs. And all during the summer months, each one of them would have a parade. They'd have a parade on Sunday afternoons and balls on Monday nights. Yeah. Well, in them days you had Kenny's Hall, which was a dance hall. And you had the old Masonic Hall, where it was at Rampart and the corner of Pedita. And Kenny's Hall was on Pedita between Liberty and Franklin. Well, I can't use the expression that they used to call these old Halls, but anyhow. My guard mother used to take me there when I was a kid.
Yeah.

And them days, Bunk Johnson was playing there. That was on Saturday nights. Every Saturday night they had a dance sometime, they'd have them on Sunday nights. Remember who was with Bunk in that family? No, because I was too small. See, I was too small at that time to remember who was playing with them.
But just the sixth grade was...

Well, anyway, I think it was Bunk Johnson. And, well, Lurie was small at that time, too. We used to play together, and most of the time Lurie used to always be fooling around with the horn. Yeah. Well, in them days it was cornets. It wasn't trumpets like the...
No, they were cornets.
It was always cornets.
Yeah.

And, well, he got his inspiration from Bunk. And I got my inspiration from Henry Martin, Black Benny, Red Happy, Baby Dodds. But Baby Dodds used to play in the Orleans during them times. Yeah. Well, after I got old enough I used to go to dances. I, wherever Baby Dodds was playing I was always there. And actually I got a lot from, learned a lot from him. Oh, sure. Yeah. Well, when I, around 1918, I was taking press roll lessons from Henry Martin. Yeah. He was a left-hander like me.
Yeah.

And I used to go and take press rolls and learn the beats and different things. He wasn't learning how to read or anything like that. No. Because he told me it wasn't necessary. Yeah. But anyway, I used to learn the beats and the press rolls from him. And around 1919, I bought my first set of drums. Hmm. I bought them from Woodrisse and direct from the factory. Yeah. In them days, he was using overhanging pedals, side cymbal, Chinese tum-tum, one cymbal, snatched drum, and a drum stand.
That's what your first kid outfit?

That was my first outfit, yeah. Yeah. Well, most of them was made of wood. They wasn't like they are nowadays. Yeah. But the drums they got nowadays, much heavier than you was. It was very light because I used to walk from Iberville and Galvis all the way down to Old Bourbon and Roma somewhere along down and then play music.
Yeah. Was it a very expensive outfit, the first one you had?
No. I think I paid around about a hundred and some odd dollars for the whole outfit.
Yeah.
It wasn't nothing expensive. Well, at that time, I was living down at Aunt Johnson and La Perouse.
Mm-hmm.
Well, I was working at the Witten National Bank on the night.
Mm-hmm.

Well, after I'd get up in the daytime, wash up and eat, I'd sit down and practice with a little 10 cents gazoot. Oh, yeah. Yeah. And that's how I learned myself how to set my time and everything from what I've heard, Baby Dots and Henry Martin and Red Happy used to do. Yeah. Because a lot of time I used to go to the Lyrics Theater when the old Professor Joe Robichow was playing at the old Lyrics Theater. Yeah. Well, Happy was on drums and then one time he had Black Benny on drums with him. Oh, yeah. Well, Black Benny was more of a showman than Red Happy was. Yeah. Because he was always doing the sticks up and then, catching them on the beat and everything, you know? Yeah. Yeah. And so I used to do that every day when I got up in the afternoon.
Yeah.
And I just kept that up until I moved back up to Ivoryville and Galvis. And I started out playing with piano.
Mm-hmm.
And he was a boyfriend of mine, he was a drummer with him and I was right around the corner from my house. I don't care, I was between Biemble and Ivoryville.
Yeah.

Well, every Sunday they used to have yard parties. Mm-hmm. And they used to hire him and I because we was best at a lot at that time. Well, he had several other little outfits and then we had a boy from down on Parker, down on Parker Street that we called Frog. Well, he was very fat, he was much stoutier than Dick is.
Mm-hmm.

Well, he had a little kazoo made in the form of a cornet. Yeah, yeah. And you could be two blocks away at night and hear that boy blowing that thing and you'd swear that somebody would a trumpet. Yeah, yeah. Well, we formed that little combo and there was nobody to touch us at that time. Well, all during the meantime I was getting my beats together, you understand what I mean? Because a lot of the boys was out on drums, they wasn't getting their beats together, nothing like that. They were just playing mostly for the fun of it. Yeah. Well, Foster Lewis and Dude was two brothers. One was Foster Lewis with trombone and Dude was a trumpet player. Yeah, wow. And Bud Russel was a bass player with him. So I had him to come set in with us several thunders, you know, to give, help to give a good pep to the band, you know? Yeah, right. Kind of pep them up some.
Who else was in the band, you remember?

Well, there was Bud Russel, Baby Brewster, and this boy Frog and myself, it was four of us. Yeah. Well, we didn't say hi to Russel because he didn't want to be hired out, you know, because he was already with this other band. And, well, we played practically all over the city on Sunday nights, but our main headquarters was up here at Galveston, the Iberville.
Oh, yeah.

Well, we used to play there most Sundays than any other place. Well, Bud Russel took me in the band with them. Eddie Dawson was on banjo, Bud Russel on bass, Fausté on trombone, Dude on trumpet. And we had a fella used to call yellow on saxophone. And I forget the banjo player. He's a little bit of short fella. I think they call him Dad. Little Dad? Yeah.
By that's when something?

Yeah, it's kind of hard of hearing. Yeah. But we had him on banjo. Well, I played with Bud and them for several years. Sometime Eddie Dawson, he'd play bass with us or either play banjo with us. He's still working for the Whitneyette. And he used to play sometime with us too.
You still had the same drum outfit then? No, no.
I got a new outfit altogether. I paid, all together I paid 400 some odd dollars for what I got right now. Yeah.
What year was that about? Because it's an Irish set. What year was it about that you was with this band?
Oh, that was around 1920, 21, 22, around the name. And the set of the outfit I got now paid for about 400, about $500 for it. Yeah. It's an Irish set, you know?
Yeah, that's it, yeah.

Well, I don't use all the chaps that the present day drum is used because if you're gonna play authentic, you've got half authentic stuff with you, see? What's the only thing that's missing is the side cymbal on the bass drum.
Yeah, yeah.
But that's my cymbal, tom-tom, and all the rest of the equipment, well I got that.
Yeah, those side cymbals, like they would be to…

They would be attached to the side of the bass drum. Yeah. And they had a little ball, metal ball, that you could throw on to hit the cymbal and you could throw off just for the bass drum. Yeah. Well that's when you was gonna play soft, you'd throw that metal ball off and the main ball would be hitting right on the head of the bass drum.
Yeah, yeah, I getcha.

See? Well that was when you was getting soft and when you was ready to break it down going out, then you'd take your stick and throw that metal back for the cymbal and the board up and hit it at the same time. Yeah, hit it at the same time the bass drum pedal and the cymbal. Yeah, that's right.
That's right.

Well naturally all that went out of style, we had to get margin, but I don't say I'm a, what you call a margin drummer, I'm mostly authentic because we play all the authentic numbers and I use authentic equipment as much as possible, just the side cymbals missing.
Yeah. You never used tom cymbals?

No, I never used a hi-hat at no time. No, no. Because see in them days they never used hi-hats. No, no. And it's not necessary for, you use hi-hats and it gives a nice swing, I'll admit to that. It really gives a wonderful swing, but that's alright for these big bands, you understand what I mean? But for a small outfit like we got, we don't exactly need a hi-hat.
So you never used that at any time?
Because I get practically the same effect out of that one cymbal that I can get out of using a hi-hat. Yeah.
But you never used a hi-hat at any time?

No, not at any time. No, not at any time. Not no time, because I never did buy any. I had one outfit was given to me and I gave it away because it wasn't necessary that I'd use it because I wasn't accustomed to it. I'd have to start learning all over again with the hi-hat for one beat and the bass drum for one beat is more than one beat altogether with them two different outfits, you see?
Yeah.
So I get quite the same effect I get out of the one cymbal, you know?
Yeah, that's right. But say these other drummers, like Black Benny and that, they wouldn't have sock cymbals in those? No, they never used none either.
Baby Dots never used none either.
No. When was about the first time you saw a sock cymbal being used?

Well, the first time I saw a sock cymbal being used was around the year of 1930. That was the first time I seen a muse. That was in New Orleans? Yeah, right here in New Orleans. That was the first time I saw a muse.
Remember who was the guy that was used?
No, I think I had saw him. I didn't know who the fella was, but it was a ball I went to and I saw him using that hi-hat.
And they were just the same, just the same way, the same make, sort of?

Yeah, it is, yeah, the same make. Same height? But some of them, the bell was a little bit deep on the top cymbal, you know what I mean? Oh, yeah. But now they're practically both about the same thing now, they're a little bit flatter now.
Yeah, yeah.

And that was the first time I got a chance to see them using those, what we call them sock cymbals. Yeah, that's actually it. So I never really bothered with none, I said because it wasn't necessary to be carrying all that around no, huh? Because you see, a jazz, an authentic jazz drummer, he's got numbers to play that he's got to use his sticky hit on the bass drum. Yeah. Like two beats or maybe an explosion beat, something like that, you understand? Well that's hard to concentrate with a sock cymbal. Yeah, I guess so. Because I tried when I had that, when I had it, I tried to work it out, I said now when you come to a full four to beat, that's where you're going to catch it. Or to a full four beat, you understand what I mean? Yeah. You're going to catch the devil, you've got this foot going on one beat and this one going on a full four.
Yeah, that's it, yeah.

Well that's really hard. But if you pay attention, you notice all of these drummers that's using these hi-hats, they're not beating no full four beat with that other foot. No. They got it hi-hat. You see, it's a one on each one of them. One foot going one time, another foot going the other time, see? Yeah, that's right. And naturally, they try to get on a full four beat with that sock cymbal, somebody go get messed up somewhere. Because I was doing that one day we was having a hoist, and I had this foot going like I was playing a pair of sock cymbal, and Joe said, no Joe, don't do that. I said, you're going to mess yourself up. Yeah, yeah. I said, because you're on a full four beat. That's right. I said, it's all right with one beat numbers, you know, and something like that. But most of the time you take like, Musrat Ramble or a number you all called a little while ago, that Collegiate.
Yeah, Collegiate.
And some of the old standard numbers, well they all called for one beat.
Yeah.

You see? Sometimes you have to pick up first, you got to be the first man to hit a two beat. But sometimes the trombone here coming out with his two beats, and you pick up right behind him. Yeah. Well it's hard to do that with a sock cymbal.
Yeah, I guess.
You see? You know, you have to hold a level mind, which is hard to hold a level mind for a man that's playing a sock cymbal in a four four beat on a number.
Yeah. See how?
Can I stop you for a minute?
Yeah. Well, say with the earlier drummers, you know, like Black Benny and Louis Cartrell, see? Did they play more of the same stuff as you're playing today, sort of?

No. Well, yeah, Black Benny did. Yeah. But you see, Louis Cartrell, he did more reading. Yeah. He got his, he done his most of the reading, not from, not from, from the ear. Yeah. And Black Benny, well, he never did read. No. Yeah. But he take a lesson here in the morning like I did. That's where he learned his beats. Yeah.
But they use more or less the same press roll beats then?

Oh yeah, same press rolls. Yeah, they use most of the, more, use that more or less. Yeah. Which you take all jazz drummers, always use a press roll. Yeah. But you'd rather sell them if you notice any big bands or any small combos. You never catch the drummers using press rolls.
No.
We was up in Indianapolis one time and they had a 17 piece outfit.
Mm-hmm.
And I was setting my drums up and I was making a press roll, you know, tuning my drum up.
Mm-hmm.

And they had a young drummer and he came back behind the curtain and asked him, said, how do you do that? I said, do what? He said, make that roll. Mm-hmm. I said, press roll? He said, that's what they call it? I said, yeah. Mm-hmm. Well, I couldn't understand it. It saved my life. A person playing drums with a big outfit like that couldn't make a press roll. So I gave him the sticks and I showed him. I said, now you just roll them. I said, it's in trouble. I said, practically it comes from the wrist. Yeah. And I said, you just roll it on your drum. I said, your music. I said, on your sheet music it tells you when to make the rolls and all, you know? Mm-hmm. Because I had taken, not a full lesson, but when Paul Barbrain used to come by my house, he is showing me how to read notes and how to make rolls. Well, I already knew how to make rolls because Henry Martin had done learning me already. Yeah. And I was taking a few lessons from him. So he told me, he said, well, it ain't necessary. He said, you're going to play jazz drumming. I said, yeah, I'm just going to stick to jazz. I ain't going to play nothing else. I don't care what happened, what come out. I'm just going to stick to the old time stuff if they continue to play it during the future,
you know?
I see. Yeah. So things had got kind of tough for music and I gave it up for a while. That was back in the 20s. Yeah.
So I gave it up for a long time.
What was the last job you played? Do you remember?
The last job I played was up in the Irish Channel.
That was back in the 20s, late 20s. Well, after that music kind of died down and I gave it up. But I was still doing night work with the National Bank.
Yeah.

So I sold my outfit I had. Yeah. So after I got married and moved down here, I was over across the street at 825. Yeah. Well that was during the days of Mo Rambles, Mo Rambles, who had Mo Rambles, I know who heard of him. Oh yeah. The trumpet player. Well Walter Nelson, he's down here at the Piku's place, he plays steel guitar. Yeah. Him and I had met one night up on Bama Street by some friends of ours and he was playing his guitar and I was passing my foot in tempo with him, you know. He said, Joe, do you ever play music? I said, yeah, I play drums. I said, I used to play drums but I don't play it now. I said, because business has been kind of bad and I just sold my drums and gave up.
Yeah.

He said, why don't you start back again? I said, I don't have no outfit to start with. He said, well, the Rambles one, or buy a second handed outfit. He said, I can always use a drummer. I said, well, all right. So I went somewhere and bought a second hand outfit piece by piece, you know. Yeah. And he started getting a few little jobs lined up. So one night him and Moran and myself played back in Gentilek, three pieces. Well, I played so well that night after being off for so many years. And I said, well, Ed Moran told me, he said, Joey, you go stick with them drums. I said, I'm going to try. He said, don't give them up. He said, hang on to him. He said, we'll get enough working with a larger band as we go along. I said, well, all right, whoever, I said, I'll hold on to him. Well, I was working in the daytime there at the bank. I switched from night porter to day porter. I said, well, I'll hold on to him until I get a better outfit.
Yeah.
So sure enough, we started getting plenty of work and we enlarged the band. What year was this about?
Six pieces.

That was around the thirties. Oh, yeah. The early thirties? No, no, forties. Oh, yeah. That's around 1941. Yeah. And I was over there at the time. Yeah. And we started getting plenty of work then. And we started to hire more men. Well, we played down here at the old Silver Star, down at St. Bernard and St. Claude. And we played down there for a couple of years on Friday, Saturdays and Sundays. Do you remember the rest of the band?
Who was in the rest of the band? No, I don't care.
There were so many different fellas, because every week we weren't able to get the same
men.
But I know for one while there we had George Lewis and Slowdrag with us.
Yeah.
Well, they played a while with us until we got caught in the red and then we'd get the job up because we didn't like that idea, you know?
Yeah, yeah.

So we started playing down in the little country parishes. And every Sunday during the summer they had picnics down there where we'd go and they'd hire us to play the picnics. Yeah. It was mostly colored picnics and everything else. So one night, you know one Sunday afternoon, Eddie Morris needed a drummer. He was playing out here on Canal Boulevard at Linford's.
Yeah.
And he needed a drummer and he told Slowdrag to see if Slowdrag could get in touch with me. Yeah. And told me to come out there.
Yeah.
So I went on out there and I played with him. And in the meantime Slowdrag came back and asked if I had got home.
Yeah.
My wife told him no I had knocked off. And he said well as soon as he come home, tell him that George wants him to play with him tonight right at the corner from my house.
Yeah.

So sure enough when I got home she gave me a message and I went on out there and all us George, Lawrence, Drag and myself, four of us, we played a house party there for them. Yeah. Some white people that lived right at the corner from Drag's house. The following week George had another job for me playing at the St. Mary's Church front out there. We played that. The following week he had a job to play an advertising for a prize fight back at Pelican
Park. Yeah.

So that night he told me, he said, George, how would you like to work regularly with me? He said I'll get in the playing of work. I said well, I said George I'll tell you. I've been off these things so long and I'm trying to get back into them. He said well I think you're doing nicely. He said I want you to play with me, he said because you've got that old style of playing that I like. He said because I'm not going to change the none of this modern stuff they're playing. He said I'm holding on to the authentic. And they said you play the authentic drums? I said yeah I want. Yeah. So from then on I was playing all the jobs with him. Yeah. We went back to his hard out at Manus Tavern back on Benefit and St. Rock. We played out there, oh I forgot how many years, on Friday, Saturday and Sunday nights. Well that's where a lot of the people from in town was coming back at, back there after they heard about George Lewis where he was playing every weekend. So from there Nick Gagliano had taken over the band.
Yeah.
And he got us to work steady out at El Morroco, that was back in 1950.
That's on Bourbon and Iberville.
Bourbon and Iberville, yeah.
Well we worked there for a couple of years. Who do you have in the band then?
Well we had Talbot, Slow Drag, Elton Pornell, George Lewis, Lawrence Moreira and myself. That was the old regular lineup.
Yeah.

No trombone? Yeah, Jim Robinson. Oh Jim, yeah. Well we stayed there for about two years I'd say. Yeah. Then Reverend Kershaw in the meantime when we was playing out there they came down here and heard different bands and they selected our band.
Mm-hmm.
And this fella Hank from Chicago, he heard us after El Morroco.
Mm-hmm.

Well I think first we went to Cincinnati, Ohio, then into Oxford and then after that we started traveling around because Hank got us out to Chicago and that's how the band got on the road. Start to travel around different places and the first thing you know we was going to California. So how we come to go out there this woman had heard about us, Rose Stammon and she had wrote Nick Gagliana and they started negotiating about the band. So George got us all together and asked us how we liked her. But we all agreed to go you know mostly for the trip anyhow. Yeah, yeah. Well after we started working for her then work started coming regular out there. Yeah. Well we must have played Los Angeles about a dozen times I guess.
This was still with the same band with El Morroco.
Yeah, yeah. No Talbot wasn't with us. Talbot died in 50. Oh yeah. Yeah, he died in December of 1950.
That was when you were at the El Morroco still. Yeah, after we left there yeah. Yeah.
We had, oh what this guy's name, played trumpet with Paul Ballbrand sometime. Oh I can't think of his name right now because he only played such a short time with us.
Yeah.

Then after that we had Kid Howard with us. Oh yeah. Well he made several trips out there with us. Tom Jefferson he worked out there with us. Yeah. Then we had him in Frisco, we had Howard in Frisco too. Well they were switching about you know. Yeah, yeah.
The first trumpet player that you had in George's band then was El Morroco Talbot.

El Morroco Talbot yeah. It was the first one. Yeah, it was after I started playing with him. That's the first record trumpet man he had. You never played with him with Bunk? No, no, no, not at no time no. So you never played with Bunk? Because I, when I was playing with George at Silver Star. Yeah. That was when he went with Bunk to New York in 1945 or 44, 45 I think it was. Yeah. Because it was in 46 that I joined up with the band after they finished in New York. Well anyway to get back to California trips. Yeah. The last time we played for Rose Stanley we had Howard with us. Yeah. Well she had solo plays and we went back with Tom Jefferson to play for this fella that's got it now.
Yeah. I can't think of his name.

I can't think of his name. He's a little Jewish fella. I can't think of his name right now. But anyhow we made a couple of engagements for him. We played at the Tin Angel in San Francisco. Oh yeah. We played that about three times, nine months in all. Then we played for, for Doc Dorothy at the Hangover. Yeah. Played for him a couple of times.
That was when Lizzie Miles and Joe Robertson came out there. That's right, yeah.
Well I think that was the last engagement that we played, excuse me, that we played for him was when she was out there.
Yeah.
Well things that got kind of tough with me around 1955, Doc was getting up a house band. Well he had, what's his bass player, he used to play with Ori. Barlin Burden.
Barlin Burden. Garlin.

Oh, Ed Garlin, yeah. Well Ed Garlin had wrote me a letter and asked me about playing well and I told him he asked me because our band wasn't doing anything and I was willing to, you know, take the job until I could make a pretty good salary. So Doc had called me on long distance phone and told me, asked me how I'm ready if I wanted to come by plane or by train. I told him not before to come by train. So he sent me a ticket and I went on out there and that was August, the latter part of August 1955. Yeah. Because I opened up on a Labor Day night with Earl Hines. Oh yeah, you were playing with Earl Hines. So I played out there six weeks with Earl.
Who else was in the band then?

Earl had Ed Garlin, Earl Hines, and this little white trumpet player there, I can't think of his name. Muggsy was it? No, it wasn't Muggsy Spaniel, no. Another little trumpet player, he's pretty bad off sick now if he ain't dead now. He's out there in San Francisco. And we had this clarinet player, Donnell Howard. Oh man. Our clarinet. We only had a six piece lineup. Earl Hines, Donnell Howard, Ed Garlin, myself. You were on trombone. And Lil' Jimmy.
Jimmy Archie? Lil' Jimmy Archie, yeah.

He was on trombone. I think he's still with Earl Hines, if I'm not mistaken. But he wasn't on that concert at Monterey, I think he was still at Muggsy Spaniel at the Hangover. Yeah. So you worked there for what, six weeks? See I worked with him for six weeks and they got this boy Earl Watkins to take my place. Because see my type of drumming and Earl's type of music didn't fit in together. See because I was, just like I said, I was more on the authentic side than what he was. Because he was kind of swinging his band more, you know.
And this Earl Watkins was playing the more modern stuff.

Yeah, he was playing the modern stuff. So naturally hired him, which didn't make me angry at all because I just had an idea I wasn't going to make it after the first two weeks with him. You know, I just didn't watch this. You're watching this is it. You just working on Back to the Army. Well, George was out there when I started playing with him. Yeah, Lawrence's cousin Si on drums then. Si Frazier?
Yeah, Si Frazier.

Well he was on drums, he had taken my place. So I told George, I said, well I'm going to pass through Los Angeles and I'll drop by and see y'all on my way home. So, I stopped over that night and I checked my drums in and come here to New Orleans. So I stopped at the Watkins Hotel and I went on back, went on out to the tavern where George and him was playing. Yeah.
Remember the name of the tavern? Yeah, Beverly Caverns.

Oh, Beverly Caverns. Yeah, Beverly Caverns. So, I went on over there and stayed there back there all night with him. So, Si asked me, say, Joe, you want your job back? I said, I ain't coming here for my job. I said, I'm going home. He said, no, I want you to take it back. He said, because my wife wrote me a letter and told me that she got a letter from the civil service and I'm going to work for civil service. I said, well, in that case, I said, you speak to George and whatever George says, I said, it's all right with me. So, George said it was all right with him. He said, regardless, he said, y'all two get your head together and just make up your minds, whatever you want to do. So, Si said, no, he said, you go ahead and take the job back. He said, well, I'm going back home. I said, well, I'll let you have my ticket at a cheap price. So, I sold him my ticket for $25. How was he playing at the time, Si? He was playing all right. He fitted him with the band. Yeah, he fitted him pretty good with the band.
Was he using a sock symbol or anything?
I didn't, I don't think Si used a sock symbol.
But he was using a normal, sort of New Orleans press roll beats and everything. Oh yeah, yeah, he used that plenty.
He's something like me, he used that plenty. Yeah, that's it. So, I caught him.
Wait a minute, let me put on here. This is Rio 2, Joe Watkins, January 20th, 1961.
Okay, so we got up to about when Saeed was going late when Saeed came back.

Yeah, so Saeed left and I had to go to the station to order my drums back. They was on the way to New Orleans when I got there the following day, so they shipped them on back to me. And I taken over and we finished playing out there about two months afterwards. And we came on back home. But things had got kind of rough, peak, you know? Well, we played several little jobs around town.
Yeah.
House parties and different things like that up around the rich people uptown, you know? Who was on trumpet at that time? Well, we had Howard with us.
Still Howard. Yeah. Still the same band as Lawrence.

Mm-hmm. Yeah. Yeah, Lawrence was with us. That was the time Lawrence was taking sick. Oh, yeah, yeah. Yeah. You had that trombosis of the brain. Yeah. Well, that happened out there in Hollywood. Mm-hmm. Well, we was living in Hollywood, but we was playing at the Beverly Caverns.
Yeah.
And after he'd taken sick that first time, when we went back out there again, the same thing happened. Mm-hmm. Well, he had caught himself, because we were just playing the last number, the last set.
Yeah.

When he was about to keel over. Mm-hmm. And he caught himself, you know? And he stopped playing, and George told him to take his banjo and go ahead in the back. Yeah. So, that was the last job we played out there. Yeah. And ever since that, well, things had been kind of on the down grid, and then we started going back out to Cincinnati. We started working at the Sinton Hotel on weekends.
Yeah.

Well, we'd done that for quite a long time. And I guess you came back then, you made the English trip, did you? Yeah, it was, yeah, we went, it was from there. And we was working at the Sinton Hotel. Mm-hmm. When we got news that we was going overseas. Mm-hmm. So, we came on back home after we finished the engagement with Andrew Sinton. We came back home, that's the time I was trying to find Russell. Yeah. To see if I get our passport. Passport. Because George had his, you see. Yeah. Whether it was Jack, Howard, Jim, Joe Robichaud, and myself that had to get passports. When did Joe Robichaud come in and Purnell leave? Well, that was after Purnell had stayed out in Frisco. Yeah. You see, that was the time that George first went overseas by himself. Yeah. That was back in 56. Yeah, that's about it, yeah. Yeah. Because at that time, we was playing at Tin Angel. Yeah. And out and stayed out on the West Coast. Yeah, he stayed out on the West Coast then with it to finish out, you know. And he said he was going to decide to stay out in Los Angeles. I said, well, Elton, I said, it's up to you. I said, you do the suit yourself. But I said, the rest of the band is going back home. I said, because nothing to us is staying out here. I said, our families is back home. It's better that we going back. Well, at that time we had Bob Thomas on the trombone and Tom Jefferson on trumpet.
That was the band that made those records on Cavalier, remember? Yeah, Cavalier.
Yeah, that's another record I miss getting. I never did get a chance of getting one.
That was without Lawrence though, you know?
Yeah, that was without Lawrence.
So how did you feel when Lawrence wasn't there? Did you play any different, say, without the band?

I miss him a lot in a way because him and I was always kidding one another, you know? Yeah. What if I kind of get off the beat a little bit, he'd give me a wink, you know? If I was too fast or a little behind on the beat. That's one thing I like about it. He'd always advise you if you was ahead of your time, you know? Yeah. I knew he was a little good timekeeper. Yeah, I used to listen mostly to him. And I kept my beat straight a lot, but since he's not there, well I still can keep it straight because I can concentrate, you know? Yeah. Instead of trying to listen to somebody else, I can concentrate on my own self. But you didn't sort of change at all?
No, no, I didn't change, no. You played the same.

Just the same identical thing, same identical thing. Yeah. But now it's more so on the cymbal now because we don't have that banjo. You understand what I mean? Yeah, I know what you mean, yeah. Because when we had the banjo, I didn't have the word too much, I would open up a number with a cymbal. That's it. But now to get the band a full volume, well I open up on a cymbal with a number, particularly fast tempos and moderate tempos.
Yeah. Say when you first started with the band, you didn't use so many cymbal on the records, you know? No, I didn't, no. But how come then you changed to using cymbals?
Well, because that's the way George had wanted it, because he gave the band a better volume, you know?
Is that the way you felt what suited best as well? Yeah. You felt it went best along like that?

Yeah, because when I hit that fourth lick, it looked like the spirit just hit me to go right on then. Yeah. Because it starts right on the snap drum, just like George would tell me, he says, it sounds kind of dead. You understand? Yeah. It do sound dead starting off on the, on the, just on the drums instead of the cymbal, well when I, when we have a nice fast tempo, a moderate tempo, I hit right on the cymbal, and just start riding everybody in a full swing.

I guess another thing would be that the cymbals are very good cymbals now you can beat, like in the old days they probably couldn't beat out cymbals because the cymbals weren't very good cymbals. No they wasn't, no they wasn't. So it wouldn't suit to be beating out cymbals in the old bass.
See I have a, I have a zillion cymbal and I have one of those river cymbals.
Yeah.
Well I tried that river cymbal a lot, it's alright in a way, but it's alright for them big bands.
Yeah.

You see because it doesn't hold the volume like you want on a, on a real zillion cymbal. You see my, my big zillion cymbal is like that. What size is it? I think it's eighteen. Oh yeah, eighteen. Eighteen inch cymbal. And I think my river cymbal is about the same thing.
Yeah.
Well I just bought the thing, I paid forty some more dollars for it and it's still there up in the room and I was trying to sell it but I can't get nobody to buy it you know. Yeah.
I'll tell you, another thing I was going to ask you about, you've been singing a lot on George's records and that. Oh yeah. How you come along taking the singing you know?
Well I'll tell you how I come to do that. When we was playing back at Manny's, I'd take it upon myself and I'd take it upon myself to sing to help them out. Yeah.
You understand what I mean?

Yeah. Because I know they needed a lot of rest, you take the men like they're blowing. Well we didn't have no piano. Yeah. Back there at that time. So naturally I'd take them to sing it so the man decided to get a piano to fill in. Well he got a piano and George got hired Elton to play with us. Yeah. So from then on I've been doing the vocals.
But you never got no singing lessons did you? Never taken a lesson in the day of my life. But you just sort of felt that you'd sing.
I just picked it up, just picked it up. I said well if my dad was a good song so I would be able to sing too.
Yeah.
Because he was one of the best bass vocals we had in the third ward when I was a kid.
So you've been singing pretty long.
So I figured from then I said well if he could do it I'm going to try it too. So naturally I've been singing ever since.
Remember what was the first number you sang with George's band?
No I really don't. I guess you sang a little band. But I do know we had some very unusual numbers I used to do right there. I remember that well. You remember that eh?
Down on the farm?
Yeah, down on the farm boy I'm telling you man.
You thought I was a itty bitty boy?

Yes indeed. And the. See down on the farm and some other little rashes number we had we used to sing back then. Well there was several, naturally the customers went for it, but naturally I was going to keep on singing them you know.
Yeah.
Because they was always requesting it so naturally I sang it. And one while I played with Joe Thomas back on St. Bernard in Russia playing.
Yeah.
He was playing back there. Yeah.

See on this record you know where you play the Spiritus you play the wire brushes. Yeah. And two beat on the bass drum. Yeah that's right. But this is the first time you ever played in the church was it?
First time.
Yeah. First time the whole band in fact. Yeah. How come that you used the brushes on all them? You just thought that would fit the edge?
Well it was kind of softened down a little bit instead of using the sticks.
But you never heard anybody use these uh, play this way in churches when you were young?
No.
Uh-uh.

Never did. Never heard of a jazz band in my life being in the church. Yeah. Never heard of a jazz band in Oakland of the spiritual, felt like I was on a string. See? Yeah. But that actual wire brush and two beat on that, you never heard that before? No, no. That was just something I had this big...
I've heard quite a few people doing that now.

Yeah, I see. I've got to do something to kind of keep the volume down low under my singing, you know, and under their mutes. Because you can't get the exact riff out of sticks like you want, like you can't get out the brushes. Yeah, I know what you mean. So you see the brushes give a kind of a sweeping effect. Yeah.

Well, it's on these records. Something I was going to ask you. Remember on this, these disc jockeys you made? Yeah. And you made this funeral sequence on there? Yeah. When Lawrence plays the bass drum. Did he have his own bass drum there? Or was he playing... No, he had his own bass drum. Yeah, he brought his own bass drum.

Yeah. And he had his own bass drum. But there was some other place... There was some other place that he used my bass drum on a sequence like that. I forgot where it's at. But there was no recording of it. But see, that wasn't on the recording. That was his own, that was his own little bass drum he had. Yeah. And you had your regular snare drum on that?
Yeah, my regular snare drum, yeah. You were sitting there playing your regular snare drum.
And I had my belt and all. Oh yeah, you were sitting there. Because Nick had told us to bring them along with us, you know? Yeah. Yeah, I get you.

And still on these records, well, on this one, someone I'll be meaning to ask you. Where is it? Is he on that one, Dr. Jazz? Uh-huh. Well, you sing on that. Yeah. And on that, the drums is terribly seem to be over recorded, you know? They seem to be loud around the rest. Yeah, yeah it was.

You figure that's, yeah. Yeah. You know that guy, he had that mic. Mm-hmm. See, it's one of the tall mics, you know? Yeah. Because he was up on the stand. Yeah. And he had it protruding too close. Mm-hmm. Because see, I was right in the center. See, George, George and, uh, Howard and Jim was on this side of me. Yeah, that's on the right hand side. And, uh, Elton was on that side. Mm-hmm. And drag and drag was on this side of me. Right. On the left. See, well, naturally, he was picking up more volume with that drum than anything else.
I guess he had it near for you to sing.

Because if you notice in particular, where I take a drum on, drum solo, on Maman on loud, you notice that roll kind of gets offbeat. Yeah. Yeah. And I didn't like that too much. No. See, but what I was gonna do, I couldn't tell him to retake it, because I didn't know how it came out. Yeah, yeah. But I do know he had that mic extended too far.
Yeah.
Up on that stage. If he'd have stayed out where he was, like this stage here. Yeah. And the mic would be over there, and I'd be back here where I'm at. Yeah. Well, it wouldn't pick me up too much.

Mm-hmm. You see? So, for— Just at the right bottom. Yeah. For the people at the front, I mean, the drum, where you was playing on that, that wouldn't have sounded no louder than usual. No, no, no. Just playing— Just playing— It was just that mic was picking it up. Yeah. I guess the mic was there for you to sing the vocal on.

Yeah, that's right. It was there for me to sing the vocal. Instead of him getting it back when it come from my solo, well, he just left it stay right there, and all I was doing was picking up that that pressure on the drums that I was making.

Yeah, that's it. Yeah. A lot of the records, it seems, you know, when you're going to take a vocal, it sounds as if the drums is playing very loud, you know. Yeah, that's right. And it's probably that the mic is hanging there, I suppose. Yeah. You had to put the mic a little too close. Yeah. Going back to this depression, you know, when you had to give up. Yeah, around the 20s. Yeah, you remember Howard was playing pretty good then, and he kept going through the—
Yeah, Howard was really wonderful during them days, because I remember one time Bud Brucell and Foster Lewis had an engagement for the Oddfellas over in Biloxi, Mississippi.
Mm-hmm.
And Howard, he had a job for some other organization over there.
Yeah.
Well, we had an advertisement that Sunday.
Mm-hmm.

See, we had to play an advertisement that Sunday afternoon and— Yeah. And play the dance that night. Mm-hmm. But Howard had eight pieces then. Mm-hmm. And we run into each other. And I'm telling you, I'm telling you, Howard really blew. You couldn't tell the difference between him and Lewis at the time.
Yeah.
He was really blooming. He wasn't really that good. He was playing really that good at that time.
Remember who he had in his band? Didn't he?

No, I didn't know none of the men in his band, because I was just, say, starting out myself. I just probably knew some of the men in the band that I was with that particular day. Yeah. But I didn't know who Howard had with him. But he was playing, say— But I know he had a darn good band.
You remember those climax records he made for Bill?
Mm-hmm.
You know those? Yeah. Was he playing the same as that or better than that?
No, I think he was playing a little better then. Yeah?
He was playing a little better than that then. He was definitely playing better than, say, he was on the records he made with George.
Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah, I get you. Let's see. Oh, yeah. Well, I'm Howard. I hear Howard play drums. Yeah, he did that one time. How did he play? Before he picked up the trumpet. Remember? Howard played good drums. He played good drums. Yeah, he played good drums. And a lot of these musicians seem to be playing drums, you know, like, what's the guy's name, Bill Matthews, he used to play drums.
Bill Matthews used to play drums? Yeah.
And that's his brother.
His brother, Bebe Matthews, one of the best drummers you had here. You know, that was a trumpet. With the exception of, uh, Oh, no. Lloyd Cottrell.
Yeah.

That was about one of the best drummers you had here. Well, really, the best drummers that I remember they had here was Lloyd Cottrell, Baby Matthews, Baby Dodds, Henry Martin, Red Happy, and Black Benny.
Who was the drummer Two Bits? Do you remember what his name was?

Yeah, Lloyd Two Bits. Yeah, he was around the Third War, too. I forgot to mention his name. What was his drummer? He was a pretty good little drummer. I never did know his right name. All I know was Two Bits because I was small then, you know. He had a pretty good edge on him then. But he was a pretty good little drummer, too. Then we had Cook Shop Son. He was another drummer.
Oh, yeah.

And they had some other boys who played drums. I never did know his name. He was pretty good, too. But the best of my knowledge was Baby Dodds, Bill Matthews' brother. Well, I never did hear Bill play drums. But he'd always told me that he was a drummer, too.
How would Baby be playing in the early days in New Orleans? Baby Dodds? Yeah, the same stuff that he was doing, say, on the punk records? Well, he never did change.

He never changed, right? Not to my estimation, no. Was he reading music in them days? I never seen no sheet music in front of him. No. And how about, say, Zooty? Because you see, you take the drummers in them days, they never did worry about reading music.
No.

In fact, none of the musicians, I don't care what instrument you were playing, they hardly work with sheet music because they had that music in their heart and soul, and when they got a hold of a number, they had it. See, what do they just mean? There's any change that they made, what they made themselves. They wanted to make variations on their horns, well, they'd work on that, see how it's going to fit in it. If it didn't work right, well, just leave it out.
Yeah.

How was Zooty playing in them days? Do you remember? Oh, Zooty? Well, I only remember Zooty from when I was 17 years old. And that's practically where I got that 4-4 beat from. From Zooty? From Zooty. Yeah. Baby was using the 4-4 beat too? Once in a while he was using it, yeah, but Baby Dots mostly used the 1-2 beat.
Do you mean what they call, Zooty was playing what they call Memphis Time, was that it? Yeah, that's right. That's straight 4-4.

Yeah, straight 4-4 beat. Because when we played in New York, we had came when we was playing at the, oh I can't think of the name of the place, at the Palmont on Broadway. Oh yeah. It came by one night and came up and told me, see I kind of reminded him of the older days, you know? And uh, she had a beat with something similar to his, I said that's where I got it from you. Yeah. That's what's the way I got it from you. How about Sae in the early days? Well I didn't know nothing about Sae until around 47. Oh yeah, yeah. I think around that time he was playing with Papa Celestan, no, Happy was playing with Celestan at that time.
Oh Happy Goldstein, I was.
Happy Goldstein, yeah. Yeah. He was another good drummer too, Happy Goldstein. And uh, well he usually had that one, two beat too a lot of times.
Mm-hmm. So how about parades? Did you ever plan any parades?
I played one parade that was on a carnival day, and I played two parades. I played one night parade with with the Bulls organization, and I played one carnival parade, and I played one funeral.
On snare drums?
Snare drums, no bass, no snare drums. But the last thing I played was the carnival parade, and now it's finished right there. Yeah. I didn't want to have no more to do with walking.
No. So you didn't-

Which we wasn't out long, we started playing at eight o'clock in the morning, we was off at two. But I just didn't like that idea that walking was a good, because you was constantly playing all the time. Yeah. And your wrists would get weary, you know what I mean? It would get tired.
Mm-hmm.

So I said, well I'll give up this, this parade business and let's stick to my other jobs. I ain't fooling that no more. Yeah. Tell you something I was going to ask you, how George Gaino come into the band. Well George Gaino got into the band by way of Lawrence Morero.
Mm-hmm.
When Lawrence was taken sick and we had to go to Boston.
Yeah.
Well we had to send for him.
Mm-hmm. He was about the best, was he, at that time?

Yeah. And we was playing at Charles Paramount. Yeah. We had went to Boston and we came back to Charles, Charles, Charles Paramount restaurant. Yeah. And that's where Gaino finished playing out with us there.
Mm-hmm. And the record you made, you know, with George on that.
Uh, Blue Note? Blue Note, yeah. Well George was on that. Yeah. Yeah, George.
You like making that record? Yeah. It was George, the way George was playing was different from Lawrence, but I mean, did it affect you much?
No, it didn't worry me at all. I like, I enjoy this playing. You played the same sort of way. Yeah, I didn't change my type, my type of playing. I just kept the same old method.
Yeah.
And he looked like he was enjoying my drumming himself.
Yeah, yeah. Yeah.
Uh, let's see.
Let's see. Let's see that. Who would you say was the, uh, your favorite trumpet player, say, that you worked with, you know?
My favorite trumpet player. Well, for authentic jazz, that was Hurt Moran.
Hurt Moran.
Yeah. But authentic playing.
Yeah. Uh, how long had, uh, Cuckoo been playing? Do you remember how long Cuckoo had been playing? Oh, Talbot was playing a long time before I met him.

Yeah. Yeah. Because I saw him several times on that Voilishman's. Uh, playing for different dancers. Mm-hmm. He'd even sing on that truck without a mic. Yeah. Oh, man. Yeah, that was long before he had started playing with John up with us. Yeah. As he had joined up with us back as manager. See, George was taking on a man at a time. Mm-hmm. Until he finally got the sixth voice in. Mm-hmm.
And I guess, uh, your first record was with Cuckoo. Yeah, that's right. Do you remember what was the first record tonight? First trumpet player was jazz, uh, Good Time Jazz. Good Time Jazz.
Yeah, that was, uh... Willow the Weeper and Mama Don't Laugh. Willow the Weeper, Mama Don't Laugh. Is he a red wing? No, Mama Don't Laugh.
What's wrong with those, anyway?
But anyway, Cuckoo was on there.
Can I tell you?
Yeah.
Willow the Weeper, Mama Don't Laugh, I got to go like you doing in Burgundy Street.
That's right. That's them.
I know, because I helped pick out the tune. Yeah.
And, uh, after that, I guess, what did you go to the Paradox LP? You know that one with the Chic and Ole Miss?
Yeah, for Paradox, yeah. Mm-hmm. You recorded? Then we made recordings for Jazz Man. Mm-hmm. And, uh, we made recordings for Antone and Cavalier.

Mm-hmm. Did you, uh, you know, when, uh, Howard come back in the band, did your drum and change at all then? No, no. After the time? No. You played the same morris the same way whatever trumpet player.

Just kept the same method. Yeah. Uh... I see Howard was, uh, what you say, an authentic drummer himself. Yeah. And I just kept up the same method, all the different trumpet players. I never changed. Mm-hmm.
Of course, you play, uh, left-handed, um...
Yeah.
Left-footed, yeah. You almost play that way?
Lots of people wonder why I play that a way. I say, well, that's the way I learned myself.
Yeah.
I say, I was left-handed, so I just started playing the drums left-handed.
Mm-hmm. But, uh, I guess it's awkward sometimes if you want to go, uh, stand in on somebody's drums, say, you know...
I'd have to change over.
You'd have to change over, yeah.

Well, it wouldn't be if one thing had to be changed, that would be the snare drum, unless they have, uh, a jungle drum alongside of them. I'd have to make the switch, you see, put the snare drum on this side and the jungle drum on the left-hand side.

Yeah, that's a tom-tom. Yeah. You call it tom-tom. Mm-hmm. That's it. Uh, let's see. What else we got here? Uh, uh, you've always, you know, you didn't start on right or something, you just, uh, carried on playing from left, I mean, right from the start, say, left foot and left hand. Yeah. That's where I first started out. Yeah. Uh, what do you remember of Alfred Williams in the early days? Can you remember how you played the tom?
Well, most of the time that I saw Alfred Williams, he was playing parades or funerals.
Mm-hmm.
I've never, uh, as yet, as long as I've been knowing him, I've never seen him play at parties or dance or anything like that, so I couldn't tell you how he played.
Mm-hmm.
Uh, how about these, uh, single head snare drums?
Do you remember that?
Well, I never did use none of them.
How would they be a single head snare drum?
Well, it's made like a banjo. Yeah. You know, it's a single head with no bottom. Where would the snares be? The snares would be right up on the top. Oh, underneath the...

Well, I'd say you turned an ordinary snare drum up and was beating on the snare head. Yeah, that's right, that's right, that's right. Oh, yeah, I get you. Of course, a lot of the fellas would use that. John McMurray probably used that, didn't they?
Yeah.
Because when Baby was... Mm-hmm. Uh, did you ever see Baby playing in later years?
The only time I, last time I saw Baby play was when he rushed me up at, uh, at this nightclub in Chicago.
Mm-hmm.
The Hunt Club.
Oh, yeah, yeah.

Because you see, he was well known around there, you know, because he used to play in different places. Yeah. Well, that was when he was sick. He was kind of sick then. Oh, yeah. But every time we went out to Chicago before he died, he always came by and I let him set in. Yeah. And then, at that time his wrist was going bad then. Yeah. And I would let him try to work his wrist some, you know, but... Yeah. But it didn't, it didn't have to do any good to him. No. Until he'd taken that stroke and he had to go to the hospital and that was it.
Yeah.
But he could still play, I guess, pretty well. Yeah, he was playing pretty good, fast numbers, but he couldn't do nothing with slow numbers. No.
No. He did pretty good with fast numbers, but slow numbers he was handicapped. Yeah, I see. Because he couldn't make the press rolls like this. No, he couldn't make the rolls like he wanted to.
Yeah.
And the baby never changed, say, right from the time you first knew him, you know, he still playing more or less the same drum.
No, he still was the same identical thing.
Right, right after that. Tell you another couple of drummers I wanted to ask you about. Minor Hall.
Minor Hall with Kidore.
Yeah.
He's a wonderful little drummer.
Yeah. Because he would use a slow press roll. Yeah.
Yeah, he had a very slow.
Yeah.
But he used a hi-hat too. Yeah. Mm-hmm. Several times when we went out there before they finished the engagement at the Beverly Cabin, when I would go up by him, you know, and listen to him.
Yeah.
He died. Oh yeah, he died a little while back.
Yeah, he died, yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah, he was a very nice snare drum player. Yeah. I like that. You remember him in New Orleans when he was in New Orleans?
No, no, I don't remember when he was in town yet.
I said it was before your time. I don't remember that.
I just remember him from out in Los Angeles.

Yeah. So we don't hear much of you before, say you started with the George Lewis band. Is that one of the first professional jobs you played? With George. With George. Yeah. That was the first professional jobs.
You didn't get paid when you were working with Harry Moran?
Yeah. But the money wasn't much though. It was five dollars or something like that, you know. Yeah.
Yeah.
After George took me on his wing, then we started making a little more money, you know. Yeah. Did you just- Well, at that time, George's popularity was growing then too.
Yeah. Yeah.
Because he was beginning to get famous at that time. Yeah.
So did George tell you to change your drumming a bit or when you joined him, you know, were you
playing the same before?
No, he didn't tell me about changing. He told me he wanted that authentic style of beating. Yeah. But the main thing was my seating arrangement.
Yeah.

You see, I used to sit on a chair like the drums used to do long years ago. Yeah. Well, and actually you couldn't get a good violin out of your beat if you were sitting on a chair. No. So he told me to try kind of a high stool.
Yeah.
Always working back at Manners at the time. So sure enough, I got a stool. And he said, now you just rest your toes on your pedal.
Mm-hmm.
And he said, you notice you'll get a better beat.
Mm-hmm.
And that's the way I've been beating ever since, 1946.
Well, you play with your toes, uh, uh, kind of like that. Yeah, kind of like that. You see? Oh, yeah. You don't put your whole foot on it.
You see, some drummers, they got it like that. That's a good idea.
You understand what I mean? I know what you mean.
But mine is like that, my heel is up. Yeah. And I get, uh, uh, a solid beat. Yeah. That way, you understand?
Yeah.
And I can work it from my, from my ankle.
Yeah.
Because you can't put much force behind your ankle if you're going to play a full 40.
Yeah. Well, most of them though use the whole foot like that, don't they? Yeah, yeah.
Yeah, I know it's a lot of them getting a heel into. So, so sure enough, after he showed me that routine, I got it down pat.
Mm-hmm.

I said, well, that's the easiest way. Yeah. So when I got this outfit, they was making jumps throughs, then you could adjust it to any length you want, you know? So I got mine adjusted just to the right side. So when I'm beating, my foot's going like that. Yeah. A lot of people think I'm overworking this. Yeah. But I ain't overworking myself no way. Well, it's easier.
But all my work is coming from here.
From there, yeah. See? Not this one, but this one here. Yeah. My left foot's going. Yeah.
Yeah.

That's why I sit mostly to the edge of my stool when I'm playing, because that gives me a bit of relaxation. A lot of them know when I knock off, Joe, you're tired? I said, no, I'm not tired. I don't feel tired at all. Just feel beat a little bit because that stuff be dying out of me, you know, or something like that. But otherwise, I never get tired. So how? Yeah. We used to go play all day, pick it some 10 in the morning to 10 at night. 12 long hours. It never bothered me.
What was about the last job you played then, before now? Yeah.
Do you mean since I'm with George?
Uh, well, no, since you've been sick. You know, before that one was about the last job you played.

Oh, that was in Chicago in October. Yeah. Uh-huh. Yeah, that was in Chicago. October 1960. Yeah, 1960, last year. I can't remember the last job we had before we got that one. I don't think we had anything too much in 1960.
And you hope to be playing again now pretty soon?

Oh, yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. I just want them doctors at the hospital to get them my treatment so I can get my risks and actions, because I've got a barbell up there I use. Not a barbell, but an exerciser. Yeah. And, uh…
And then you'll go back and join George, I guess? Oh, yeah. Yeah. Yeah, I never quit the band. No. Because George ain't got a band now, I guess.
Well, these same men gonna stick with him. Mm-hmm. Ain't nobody gonna leave, you know. It's only drag and gymnasts out because they don't want to travel no more.
Mm-hmm.
But we're gonna travel right on.
Yeah. How do you like Joe Rubischoff's piano playing as opposed to an album?

Well, for a modern pianist, he's really good. Yeah. He's a really wonderful modern piano player. He's kind of… I don't know how to say it. He can't get into the real spirit of jazz. You know, like real jazz, hunky-tonk piano players, you know?
He's got that beat of Alton. Yeah, that's right.
And I see Alton, he's really a little… Yeah. A wonderful little jazz pianist.
Mm-hmm. And, say, before you made the English trip, Howard was playing with you regular then, or did he just sort of come back and just make that track? He was playing with us as a regular man, yeah.
Well, he had stopped for a while and we went back and got him. Mm-hmm. So we had to go over… Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.

This is Reel 3, Joe Watkins, January 20th, 1961. Right. Alright, Joe. See, I got my notebook here, but I thought of something before I got to the notebook. What about Andy Anderson? Did you ever play with him?

Well, no. I only played with Andrew twice before he went off with us this last time. Well, that was back in the 40s. We played a job with him down the 9th Ward, and somewhere else we played a job with him. I can't exactly think where it's at. Whose band was that? It was with George.
I thought he played Neomaraka with you.

No, no. He played a couple of times with us at Paddock to place Howard. What about Frog? Did you ever work with Frog or anything? No, that was the first time I would work with Frog. When? Was on his last trip to Cincinnati. Oh, cool. Yeah, the first time I would work with him.
Mm-hmm.

Played with him once before that, but that was a carnival about two years ago. Mm-hmm. A carnival a year ago, out at the old Absinthe House. Well, you know you can't get much volume out in the street in cold weather. Mm-hmm. So I didn't know really how good he could play until we went off to Cincinnati and then I found out what a real good trombone man he was. Mm-hmm. And I really must say I loved his playing. Mm-hmm.
Well, I thought he was in the El Moraco when Jim was out a couple of times. No, not when I was there.
Mm-hmm.
Ever worked with Percy Humphrey?
Yeah, several. I worked with him many times. Because he played with us back at Manners. He played with us on several other jobs. And that's a real good authentic trumpet man too. Mm-hmm.
Seems to me he came out about the time... I think it was Cuckoo, and then Moran at the El Moraco, and then Percy. No, long before that.

No, long before that huh? Because you remember when I was telling you about the... We played over in Biloxi. I think Butt Roussel had him on trumpet, I'm more than sure. Mm-hmm. He was on trumpet and his brother, Brother Earl, was on trombone. That was the first time I ever played with him. But he didn't play in the El Moraco, Percy? He might have played a couple of times in Cuckoo's place, I don't know. Mm-hmm. It's hard for me to memorize it right now. Was Moran in the El Moraco? I think he played with us one night. Mm-hmm. Yeah, I think he played with us about one night.
What about Kid Sheik? Did you ever play with him?
Yeah, I played a couple of jobs at Sheik. What was that?
Oh, that was little yard parties.
Oh, you know, down there in the Night Ward, played a couple of yard parties with him. In the 20s or recently or what? No, that was around the 40s.
Mm-hmm. But he wouldn't be at Manny's or anywhere like that with Joe or whatever, huh? Probably El Moraco, any place?
Yeah, he played at Manny's. Mm-hmm. But I don't remember, no, he never played at El Moraco with us. We played at Manny's.
Mm-hmm.
And several other little spot jobs he played with us. Mm-hmm.
What about your relatives that either sang or played music? You mentioned that before. What, that, my daddy? Yeah, your daddy.

Well, my daddy was, he used to sing in a quartet. Mm-hmm. You know, the old barbershop quartets? Mm-hmm. Back in the early hundreds. 1900s, so he was a bass songster. And he was considered one of the best that they had in the third ward. Yeah, I got it. Well, my first instrument was piano. My mother was trying to get me to learn piano. And I had a cousin that was a wonderful pianist. And he tried to learn it, but my interest was mostly in drums. Because I used to take the rungs of the chair and go around beating on the side of the fence, on the front steps, on the bottom of my mother's wash tub. And, you know, I'd done that for a few years when I was small. But after I, while I was growing up, my ambition was to become a drummer. But I knew I had to have money for learning how to read, pay for my lessons. And naturally I came from a poor family, they wasn't able to take care of them. Nothing like that for me. So back in the early 20s, I got my first set, I don't know, in my own self. You see, I was taking lessons from Martin when I was seven, when I was 21 years old. I was taking lessons from Henry Martin. And around in the latter 20s, I was taking a few lessons from Paul Barbrand, as I said before. But I didn't see no necessity of keeping it up because I didn't have no drums or anything. So I didn't sit and board, I just had to give, giving up all hopes. But every time I heard a band of music somewhere, it just kept giving me the spirit to play anyhow. So that's why I bought my own outfit, my first outfit was listen. And I learned my own self. But once you get the press roll, like you don't have no trouble. That press roll is about the hardest thing for a stiff wrist. Understand, if your wrist is stiff you just can't get the proper beat on a fresh roll.
Did you, do you remember your cousin's name?
All I knew was Feast. Feast? Feast, but I never know his full name. And he was a piano player?
Yeah, all I knew was Feast. Did he play alone or with bands or both?
No, he didn't play with no particular band. He mostly played for enjoyment of his own self. Feast.
What kind of piano would he play?
Was he a reader or was he a reader? No, he wasn't a reader, no.
He was from the ear. Just from the ear. What kind of music would he play? Ragtime. Regular ragtime.
Yeah, regular ragtime pianos. Do you remember any of his tunes?
No, but I was too small to memorize any of them. Not even.
No, I was too small to memorize any of them.
Not eating the names. No.

The only thing I could remember him playing all the time was train effects on the piano. And he done that perfect. What do they call that style today? The train effects that he did? Is it like anything they play now? Well, from them days? But these days they have all the sound effects and the sound effects.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. All that kind of stuff. Now for Boaks to Boaks Is it like anything they play now?

Well from them days, well I've never heard anybody do it outside of him on the piano. About the only one I've ever heard done any train effects on the piano. But these days they have all the sound effects and all that kind of stuff now for boats, trains, and every other little mechanical device.
What about your daddy? What was his name? Well my father, Francis Watkins. And did he sing any special songs?

Well they had them old time barbershop songs they used to sing. And just like I said, I didn't start doing any vocalizing until I started playing with George around 1946. And the first time I was taking a chance I was singing anything. Seemed as though I was doing pretty good so I started buying up copies of different songs and would mark them down in my books so I could read them off. You know when it comes time for me to sing. I've been singing vocals ever since. I've been singing vocals ever since.
You don't remember the names of any barbershop songs you daddy told?

Let's see they used to sing Sweet Emma Liner my gal. I love them old songs they used to sing. Sweet out of line. Sweet out of line. All the old time songs they had back around them times. They're about the best quartet they had back in the whole city. Who were the guys that he was singing with? Sweet Out of Line, all the old times songs they had back around them times. They're about the best quartet they had back in the whole city.
Who were the guys that he was singing with? Did you know them?
Oh, I can't recall their names now, no. I really can't recall their names.
Do you remember a drummer called Faso by the way?
Faso, yeah.
Who did he play with?
Well, he played with different bands around the third world.
He was from up there?
Yeah.
You don't remember any special particular bands? No, no, no, no, not any particular band he played with.

Well, who did 2Bix play with? He was the same thing, different bands. He didn't have no particular band he was working with. What did the 2Bix look like? Well, he was a little short fella, something like George. Kind of thin like George, too. Same color and all.
And what about Faso? What did he look like?

Well, to recall him, I've only saw Faso twice in my life. Well, I was kind of young then, because Faso was an older man. At that time, I never paid too much attention to him. I recall his color, height and size. Give me a million dollars, I couldn't place him.

See, I was wondering how, what the difference would be in the music you'd hear on Perdido Street in that neighborhood when you were living there? And up in Carlton? It's all the same. All the same, huh? Yeah, all the same. And what would you hear up in Carlton? Do you remember any of that?

He asked me, me and Ragtime, he was the Carlton in them days. And who would be playing at the bar? Well, I don't know. I know my uncle Johnny Sing said he was playing with some band up there, but I can't recall who it was, because I never heard him mention his name.
And how many guys in the band? Do you remember the band that band? It was four then, at that time, I remember. What was your uncle playing?

He didn't even have no drum with him. He was playing Ghetto at that time. Uh-huh. He was taking up banjo in later years. That's when he went with Louis. He plays occasionally at, you know, like all weekends out there in California.

Well, guys like that, they aren't good enough to work. They only work with Louis Armstrong, Jelly Roll Morton, King Oliver, and all the rest of them. And yet today they're not working. Isn't that funny?
Yeah, it is funny.
They're not good enough for this town.

Being with famous men like that, they look like they should get up plenty of work, but they don't. See, most of his work is flashing now. But he do work on Friday and Saturday and Sunday nights, I believe. On weekends out in Los Angeles. I don't know what particular spot he's working at now. I know the last I heard him and Elton's playing at one place and Buddy Burns, he's playing somewhere else. It just splits up, you know. Sometimes they come together on jobs.
Who was playing around Pedido Street when you were little?

Well, to tell you the truth, the first ones I remember outside of Bunk Johnson when I was small, outside of him was Louis Armstrong when Louis was coming up around his teens. I remember him. I remember him. Red Happy. But I don't know who was on piano. That was playing at the corner of Franklin and Pedido. On a river in downtown corner. He used to have a little honky tonk that. Well, they used to play there every Saturday night. In the meantime, Louie was driving a cold dump car. And I think that was after he got out of Jones' home. Yeah, I think that was after he came out of Jones' home.
What was the name of this town?
I don't know. I never did know the name of it. I never did bump around in them places, you know? So I never did know the name of it.
Did they have many bands in the district when you were?

Oh yeah, because I worked as a bellhop in the—talking about the Rotender Line District? Oh yeah, they had quite a few bands out there. I couldn't recall the names of them because I wasn't paying too much ticket out, too busy working. I never could get a chance to go to them because I was working at night. See, I was a bellhop in a saloon.
Well, would they have the bands in the houses or the cribs or the cabarets or what?

No, they were in cabarets. Yeah, you had Pete Lawless at Rice Cafe, you had Tom Anderson. And Lula White, she just had a piano player. And Tom Anderson. And Pete Barrett, they didn't have no band. And there was about four or five places around there that had bands working. Well, Henry Martin, the drummer I was telling you about, he used to work with Peter Bocas. Peter Bocas. Was it Peter Bocas? I think it was Peter Bocas. I used to work with Peter Bocas at the Rice Cafe. And that's at the corner of Iberville and Murray. What was Pete playing?
Do you remember? Trumpet.
Well, Cornet in them days, because Trumpet just come out around the late 30s, I believe.
Well, what's the difference between a cabaret and a nightclub and a dance hall? How did he get that in?

To tell you the truth, I didn't see much difference in it. It was all in fact the same thing with chairs and tables out on the dance floor. There's a big enough space that I'm out there for you to dance. But the majority of the nightclubs now, they don't have no dancing space. You go there, they hear the band sit at the counter and drink, or you've got space in the back there where they can put chairs and tables back there. Or you go back there and sit down and drink. There's a very few places that's got bands playing for them at night that's got a dance floor.
Do you think that changes the drum in any? Not a bit.

They still play? But I'll tell you one thing it will do. When people is dancing, it gives you more spirit to play. Particularly if you see they're enjoying theirselves. But whether you just got to sit down and entertain people and all they can do is give you applause, well there's not very much spirit to it. Because some applaud and some don't. But when you see them all get out on the dance floor and you know they're enjoying yourself, and that's why that gives you a lot of spirit. Because I've noticed a difference in that. You know when I was playing at the Paddock or in fact any of them clubs on Boydman Street, and when we get away from you and play where people could dance, I noticed a big change in your spirit. But I don't know, that's kind of a dead spirit to me, simply not looking up at the musicians playing. When they get through you applaud them. There's a lot of people go to these clubs out here that wants to dance. Now we played at the Old Silver Slipple and they had a lot of dancing there one time. When Joe Conforto had it. Well we played then. Well he had a lot of dancing. He had a space ring off for the people to dance. Well that gave us the mood to play good there too. How long ago was that? Oh that was around 19, that was back in the early 50s. Nick Agriano had us in charge then. That was around about 1953 or 54, something like that. I remember that. That was before Gene Mills Band came down here, remember? They came in right behind us.
Yeah that was quite a deal with them, you remember that? Yeah. What happened?
Yeah they told me to let them go.
Yeah they flopped in that place and then made a hit at the concert, didn't they? Yeah, it was something. You remember a fellow named Foster and his brother Dude? Yeah.

Yeah I spoke about them on the earlier reel. I used to play with them. The first band I played with was Foster Lewis and Dude. Because Roussel, or Bud Roussel was playing bass with them. That was the first band I would play with.
Who was in that band? I didn't get that straight.
I had Bud Roussel, Farstown, Dude, Yalla, Lil' Dad. Piano player? I think Lil' Arthur was on saxophone or clarinet. Lil' who?
Lil' Arthur.
Lil' slim fella, something on all the joys but he's kind of got a funny eye. Well he ain't played in a long time now.
Is that the guy that has a restaurant down on San Bernard? No.
Not Arthur Durbin? No. Well who was this Yalla?
That's what I wanted to ask you about.

Yalla was kind of a Heaviseth Wright fella. I don't know why they gave him that name of Yalla or something. Y'all ears you know. Well I played with him, he played with Foster Lewis a few times. He wasn't no record-study man. I remember him being with the band several times.
Is that the... Does he have a brother that's a doctor or something, Yalla? Is that the one? No. Was he a policeman or something?
No, you talking about Talbot. Talbot's got a brother that's a dentist.
Oh yeah.
Yeah, he's up there in Jackson Avenue if he's still there yet. Who's that?
Dr. Talbot. I wonder if Dr. Sherry was up there on.
No, not that I know of.
No.

I think Dr. Sherry was down here somewhere on Claiborne Street. I see. It's funny, I can't remember who Yalla would be or whenever I asked you. Oh no, I think that was long before your time. Yeah. Yeah, that was long before your time. When you played with Herb Moran, who did you play with the band? Well, I was Herb, Walter Nelson.
And we had one of Lauren's other cousins. who played piano.
I can't remember his name either. It was long before your time. Yeah. It was long before your time.
When you played with Herb Moran, who did you say was in that band now?
My name was Herb, Walter Nelson, and we had one of Lawrence's other cousins that played piano. I can't recall his name either.
Oh, is he related to Saeed? Yeah.
I know who you mean. Simon. Simon Fraser. Yeah, Simon Fraser. And fellow saxist comes to me now, his name was Alfred. I never knew his full name. All I knew was Alfred.
Did he play tenor, alto, or baritone? Tenor. Tenor. Any other clarinet players besides George?
No.

Oh, by the way, I wanted to ask you, since you sing so well, what about your religion? Baptist. You're a Baptist, huh? Mm-hmm. Well, where did you learn these hymns that you sing? I learned them as to George.
George taught him? Yeah.
You don't sing those in church yourself, have you? You never did? No. Uh-uh.
Uh-uh. Well, that's funny, George knows all those things. Oh, man, you don't know what I'm happy with George. George knows more different numbers and spiritual than any man I've ever seen living.
Yeah.
Some of y'all don't play anymore, like, uh, Monk used to play, Yes Lord, I'm Crippled, and sometimes my burden is hard to bear. I don't know if you'd play them.

No, he don't play them no more because, uh, some of the fellas, they don't know him, you know? Uh-huh. A lot of times people come to the unexpected and action for those numbers and, well, he knew it and I probably knew it and Howard might know it and what the balance of the other fellas don't know it. So we just let him go.
Did you ever know Pill, Crippled Pill, played clarinet?
Yeah. He lived out here in town.
I don't know where he lived. Darkfella. I never knew him. I just heard about him. I mean, uh, Phillip Quacko, he's a clarinet player who's Crippled. I thought maybe you worked with him at some point.
Yeah, I did. I think he worked a couple of times with us at the Silver Star until the time we got raided.
Well, how'd that happen?
He died.
How'd that happen you got raided?

Well, they had a flow show on that night. Oh, yeah? And, uh, some woman was in there, didn't like the way their entertainers was dressed. Didn't like the costume they had, half-naked, you know? And this fella Joe that was operating the place, he was, he was a kind of a little gangster in a sly way. He wasn't paying off the police one. Mm-hmm. So somebody reported these women in there on the flow show and they come down there that night and they raided the place and took us all to jail. Well, drag he got out right away. And this fella, you just asked about the clarinet player, he had to be playing with us that night. But they let him go. But they took Eddie Morris, Moran, and myself. I forget who we had on piano. Took four of us to jail anyhow. And, uh, slow drag, he got out right away because he had to, uh, former Mayor Mason's brother and he got him out. And my wife, she got Joe to get me out. Joe Cianelli. That was the operator of the Silver Star. So she got him to get me out. In fact, she bailed us all out. We had a tough time to get out of it though because they wanted to make a federal case out of it. And I didn't see how they would do anything like that. But I had to pay the ten dollars to get out anyhow.
Well, uh, when you went to school, did they teach music there? No.
They teach us their music there. What school did you go to? I went to Fisk and MacDonald 24. Where is Fisk? It was at the corner of Franklin and Perdita. Was that Ms. Martin's place?
Yeah. Oh, that's a place.

This fellow, Henry Martin, that I was telling you about, that was his mother's place. Oh, I see. She was taking care of it there. And I went to that school and when we moved up from Calton, I went to MacDonald number 24. I went as far to fifth grade. I played hookah so the old lady pulled me out and I went to Roy. I've been working ever since.
Well, what about Henry's family? Did he have anybody else in the family that played music?
Henry Martin?
Mm-hmm.
He had a brother they called Kutcher. He used to play piano.
Who did he play with?

He had a brother and two sisters. Yeah, he had a brother and two sisters. Two sisters. I think Ms. Martin is living yet too. The mother or the sister? No, I think they're all living. I'm more than sure Ms. Martin is living because my wife told me she saw a while back when she used to go play the Keno games. She saw Ms. Martin and one of her daughters.
