I'd like to talk to her if I could find out her right name.
I'd like to see her myself. I don't know where the devil she live at.
You find her right name and I'll find her.
Mm-hmm.
If I could find somebody in that neighborhood, I'd make that name.
Yeah.
Do you ever know Kid Shots?

Yeah, Kid Shots and I went to the same school. And he's got a cousin named Harold that plays banjo. I never didn't know Harold's full name but he plays banjo. The three of us went to fifth school together.
Yeah.
But we didn't call him Shots then. We used to call him Toodle'em. Toodle'em? Mm-hmm. I thought Toodle'em was somebody else. No, no. We used to call him Toodle'em when we was going to school.
Well, he wasn't the main Toodle'em. No, no.
It was just an area that they gave him. Yeah. Well, what about Harold?
Who did he play with?

I don't know who Harold was playing with. He was playing out here at Mama Lou's place. Out at the lakefront. Mm-hmm. But he was working out there. I don't know if he was playing anymore. I think they told me Mama Lou closed down her place or something went wrong.
Yeah.
No more music. He's not out there anymore.
It's so hard to trace people down like that. Yeah, it is.
Well, what about the Lyric Theater?
You were talking about going there. Who did you hear there?
Oh, they used to have several vaudeville companies used to come there.
Mm-hmm.

They wasn't showing no pictures at that time, mostly vaudeville. And you had the old Dolphine Theater, Boyless. Mm-hmm. I used to go there on Saturday nights when we knocked off the wood. And every week I was always in the Lyric Theater. Mm-hmm. It used to be, before the name of the Lyric, it used to be the old Greenwall Theater.
Yeah. That's right.
That's where the Palace is now. At Dolphine and Ilybill. No, wait a minute. The Lyric is at Burgundy in Ilybill. And that's where the Palace? Well, that parking lot is now.
Oh, the parking lot.
Yeah.
Like Costa Mesa and Blanche and X.
Well, that used to be the old Lyric Theater. Is it about over with Barry? Yeah, I can't remember.
What do we have, a minute or two? Yeah, a couple of minutes.
Well, who was the leader of the band?
Yeah, a couple of minutes. Oh man, Professor Joe Robeshow. Is that the...
I think it's Joe or John Robeshow.
Is that the... Yeah.

Well, he was the leader of the band then. Left handed violin. Yeah. Is he related to the Joe that played... Joe Robeshow that played piano with us, yeah. I think that's his uncle. Mm-hmm. I see. Oh, yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm.
Mm-hm.
You remember who was in Robichaux's band at the Liried?
No, the only two I remember was Black, three rather, was Black Benny, Red Happy, and Kimball, trumpet player. I mean he was their trumpet player too, believe me.
Well who came first, Black Benny or Red Happy?
No, Red Happy and then Black Benny.
I think that's the end of it now.

segments.title: Opening of the interview and date check
segments.summary: Allen and Martyn open the session at the Watkins home and settle the date as January 20, 1961.

segments.title: Born 1900 in the Third Ward: social clubs, halls and Bunk Johnson
segments.summary: Watkins gives his birth date and describes the Third Ward pleasure clubs, parades, dance halls and hearing Bunk Johnson as a child.

segments.title: Inspirations and first drum set bought in 1919
segments.summary: He names Henry Martin, Black Benny, Red Happy and Baby Dodds as models, takes press-roll lessons, and buys a first outfit around 1919.

segments.title: Teaching himself time on a kazoo and watching Robichaux's Lyric drummers
segments.summary: Working nights at the bank, he practices by day and learns from Dodds, Martin, Happy and Black Benny at the Lyric Theater.

segments.title: Yard-party combo with a drummer friend and Frog
segments.summary: He plays piano-led yard parties in his neighbourhood and forms a small combo with a fat boy called Frog who plays a cornet kazoo.

segments.title: Playing with Bud Russell, Foster Lewis and Dude
segments.summary: Bud Russell brings him into a band with Eddie Dawson, Dude, a trombonist, a saxophonist and a banjo player, working Sundays at Galvez and Iberville.

segments.title: His new drum outfit and the side cymbal on the bass drum
segments.summary: He bought a $400-500 outfit around 1920-22 and explains the old side-cymbal attachment and why he stays an authentic drummer.

segments.title: Never using a hi-hat
segments.summary: Watkins explains why he never bought a hi-hat and that earlier drummers such as Black Benny and Baby Dodds did not use one either.

segments.title: First seeing a sock cymbal and why full four-beat playing clashes with it
segments.summary: He first sees a hi-hat around 1930 and argues that for authentic jazz with bass-drum accents it is hard to use.

segments.title: Black Benny, Louis Cottrell and press rolls
segments.summary: Martyn asks how Benny and Cottrell played; Watkins says Benny never read, Cottrell did, and all used press rolls.

segments.title: A young Indianapolis drummer and learning to read from Paul Barbarin
segments.summary: He shows a big-band drummer how to make a press roll and recalls brief lessons with Paul Barbarin and Henry Martin.

segments.chapter: Giving up and returning to music
segments.title: Giving up music in the late 1920s
segments.summary: Music got tough, his last job was in the Irish Channel, and he sold his drums while continuing night work at the bank.

segments.chapter: Giving up and returning to music
segments.title: Walter Nelson gets him playing again
segments.summary: After marriage he meets steel guitarist Walter Nelson, buys a second-hand outfit and plays a trio job with Ed Moran.

segments.chapter: Giving up and returning to music
segments.title: The Silver Star, George Lewis and Slow Drag, then country picnics
segments.summary: The band grows to six pieces around 1941 and plays the Silver Star, with George Lewis and Slow Drag sitting in, then picnics in the parishes.

segments.title: Joining George Lewis's band
segments.summary: After sitting in with Eddie Morris and Lewis, Watkins is offered regular work because of his old style of playing.

segments.title: El Morocco in 1950 and the band lineup
segments.summary: Nick Gagliano gets the band steady work at El Morocco on Bourbon and Iberville with Talbot, Slow Drag, Purnell, Lewis, Marrero and Jim Robinson.

segments.title: Touring: Cincinnati, Chicago and California for Rose Stanley
segments.summary: After Reverend Kershaw and Hank hear the band, they tour Cincinnati, Oxford, Chicago and then California, playing Los Angeles often.

segments.title: Trumpeters, the Tin Angel and the Hangover in San Francisco
segments.summary: Kid Howard and Tom Jefferson join the California trips, and the band plays the Tin Angel and Doc Dougherty's Hangover.

segments.title: Six weeks with Earl Hines in San Francisco, 1955
segments.summary: Ed Garland arranges a job and Watkins opens on Labor Day with Hines, Darnell Howard and Garland, then is replaced by Earl Watkins.

segments.title: Swapping places with Cie Frazier at the Beverly Caverns
segments.summary: Passing through Los Angeles, Watkins finds Cie Frazier on drums with Lewis; Frazier hands the job back and buys his ticket.

segments.title: Lawrence Marrero's illness, Beverly Caverns and Cincinnati's Sinton Hotel
segments.summary: Back home, the band plays house parties; Marrero falls ill in Hollywood, and the band later works weekends at the Sinton Hotel.

segments.title: Passports for the English trip and Purnell staying in California
segments.summary: On the way to England the band needs passports, and he recalls Purnell staying on the West Coast and the Cavalier records.

segments.title: Playing without Lawrence Marrero
segments.summary: He misses Marrero's timekeeping but his own drumming is unchanged, though he now leans on the cymbal without a banjo.

segments.title: Why he began opening on the cymbal; Zildjian and river cymbals
segments.summary: George wanted the cymbal for volume; he compares his 18-inch Zildjian with a river cymbal.

segments.title: How he came to sing on George's records
segments.summary: He started singing at Manny's to rest the horns, his father was a bass singer, and he recalls tunes like Down on the Farm.

segments.title: Brushes and a two-beat bass drum on the spirituals
segments.summary: He used wire brushes on the church-style record to keep volume under his vocals and the muted horns.

segments.title: Marrero's bass drum and the over-recorded drums on Dr. Jazz
segments.summary: Martyn asks about the funeral sequence and why the drums sound loud; Watkins blames the engineer's vocal mic.

segments.title: Kid Howard's playing in the 1920s
segments.summary: He recalls hearing Howard blow strongly at a Biloxi job and judges him better then than on the later records.

segments.title: Best New Orleans drummers he remembers
segments.summary: He lists Cottrell, Bebe Matthews, Baby Dodds, Henry Martin, Red Happy and Black Benny, plus Two Bits and Cook Shop Son.

segments.title: Baby Dodds, Zutty and the four-four beat
segments.summary: Dodds never changed and read no music; Watkins says his four-four beat came from Zutty, and mentions Happy Goldstein.

segments.title: Parading on snare drum
segments.summary: He played only a few parades, found them tiring on the wrists, and gave them up.

segments.title: George Guesnon joins the band after Marrero's illness
segments.summary: Guesnon replaces the sick Marrero around the Boston trip and the Paramount restaurant, and plays on a Blue Note record.

segments.title: Favorite trumpeter and Elmer Talbert's early career
segments.summary: His favorite for authentic jazz was Herb Morand; he recalls hearing Talbert on advertising trucks before he joined Lewis.

segments.title: First records for Good Time Jazz, Paradox, Jazz Man and Cavalier
segments.summary: His first record was Willow the Weeper and Mama Don't Laugh, and he kept his style under every trumpeter.

segments.title: Playing left-handed and left-footed
segments.summary: He explains he learned left-handed and would have to switch the snare and tom-tom on another drummer's kit.

segments.title: Alfred Williams and single-head snare drums
segments.summary: He saw Alfred Williams only in parades and funerals, and describes the single-head snare drum.

segments.title: Baby Dodds in his later years
segments.summary: He last saw Dodds at the Hunt Club in Chicago, weakened by illness but still fast on quick tunes.

segments.title: Minor Hall
segments.summary: He praises Minor Hall's slow press roll and hi-hat use, remembering him from Los Angeles rather than New Orleans.

segments.title: First professional job with George Lewis
segments.summary: Playing with Lewis was his first professional work; earlier jobs paid about five dollars.

segments.title: Lewis's advice on a high stool, toe pedal technique and stamina
segments.summary: Lewis told him to use a high stool and rest his toes on the pedal; he describes the ankle action and long hours.

segments.title: Last job in Chicago, 1960, illness and plans to return
segments.summary: His last job was Chicago in October 1960; he is recovering and expects to return to Lewis's band.

segments.title: Joe Robichaux and Alton Purnell on piano; Kid Howard before the English trip
segments.summary: He calls Robichaux a good modern pianist and Purnell a fine jazz pianist; Howard was brought back before England.

segments.title: Andy Anderson, Frog and Percy Humphrey
segments.summary: Allen asks whom he played with; he describes few jobs with Anderson, the Cincinnati trip with Frog, and Humphrey.

segments.title: Kid Sheik
segments.summary: He played yard parties and Manny's with Kid Sheik, but not at El Morocco.

segments.title: Family music and his cousin Feast the ragtime pianist
segments.summary: His first instrument was piano, he played on household objects, and cousin Feast played ragtime and train effects.

segments.title: His father Francis Watkins and barbershop quartet songs
segments.summary: His father sang bass in a barbershop quartet, and Watkins began singing only with Lewis around 1946.

segments.title: The drummers Faso and Two Bits
segments.summary: He recalls Faso and Two Bits only vaguely as drummers in various Third Ward bands.

segments.title: Music in Carlton and his uncle who played with famous bands
segments.summary: He cannot recall bands in Carlton; he speaks of his uncle Johnny St. Cyr and the hardship of older musicians.

segments.title: Perdido Street and the Storyville cabarets
segments.summary: He recalls Bunk, Armstrong and Red Happy near Perdido and cabaret bands such as Peter Bocage's at Pete Lala's.

segments.title: Dance floors and nightclubs, the Silver Slipper
segments.summary: He says dancers lift the players' spirit, citing the Silver Slipper in the early 1950s.

segments.title: Foster Lewis and Dude's band and the player Yalla
segments.summary: He lists the first band he played with and says little of Yalla.

segments.title: Dr. Talbot's family and Herb Morand's band
segments.summary: Mistaken identity about a doctor brother; he names Herb Morand's band with Walter Nelson, Simon Frazier and a tenor player.

segments.title: Religion and the hymns he learned from George Lewis
segments.summary: He is Baptist, learned hymns from Lewis, and explains why some spirituals are no longer played.

segments.title: The Silver Star raid
segments.summary: A clarinetist played with them at the Silver Star until police raided a floor show and jailed the band.

segments.title: School at Fisk and McDonogh 24
segments.summary: He attended school at Franklin and Perdido and McDonogh 24 through the fifth grade, then went to work.

segments.title: Henry Martin's family
segments.summary: Martin's mother ran the school place; his brother Kutcher played piano, and Allen hopes to trace Miss Martin.

segments.title: Kid Shots and the banjo player Harold
segments.summary: He and Kid Shots were schoolmates; Shots' cousin Harold played banjo at Mama Lou's.

segments.title: The Lyric Theater
segments.summary: He describes the vaudeville theatre, formerly the Greenwall, and where it stood.

segments.title: Robichaux's band at the Lyric and closing
segments.summary: He recalls Professor Robichaux as left-handed violinist leading the band with Black Benny, Red Happy and Kimball; the reel ends.
